title: The formal exponential turns sums into products
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative $\mathbf Q$-algebra and $T$ an indeterminate, with the ring $R[[T]]$ of formal power series [def-weil-formal-power-series] and the formal exponential $\exp:TR[[T]]\to1+TR[[T]]$ [def-weil-power-series-exponential], defined on series with constant coefficient $0$. Then $\exp(0)=1$ and, for all $U,W\in TR[[T]]$,

$$
 \exp(U+W)=\exp(U)\exp(W).
$$

Consequently $\exp(U)$ is a unit of $R[[T]]$ with $\exp(-U)=\exp(U)^{-1}$, and for every finite family $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ in $TR[[T]]$ and every family of integers $(\varepsilon_i)_{i\in I}$,

$$
 \exp\Bigl(\sum_{i\in I}\varepsilon_iU_i\Bigr)=\prod_{i\in I}\exp(U_i)^{\varepsilon_i}.
$$

source.place: proof of Theorem 27.6, p. 156, the step 'move the inner sum outside' (used without statement); also literature/deligne-weil-I_PMIHES-1974-43.pdf, (1.5), p. 276 (passage from (1.5.2)-(1.5.3) to (1.5.4), used without statement)

proof.text:
Fix $N\geq0$ and write $[T^N]A$ for the degree-$N$ coefficient of a series $A$ [def-weil-formal-power-series]. Since $U,W\in TR[[T]]$, the Cauchy product formula shows that $U^kW^l$ has no terms below degree $k+l$. The definition [def-weil-power-series-exponential] therefore permits truncating each exponential at power $N$ when computing any coefficient of degree at most $N$. Expand $(U+W)^r=\sum_{k=0}^r\binom rk U^kW^{r-k}$ by distributivity (induction on $r$, with Pascal's recurrence); commutativity of $R$ is used here. Since $R$ is a $\mathbf Q$-algebra, $\binom rk/r!=1/(k!(r-k)!)$. Thus the following are equal finite sums:
$$
\begin{aligned}
[T^N]\exp(U+W)
&=\sum_{r=0}^N\sum_{k=0}^r\frac{[T^N](U^kW^{r-k})}{k!(r-k)!}\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^N\sum_{l=0}^N\frac{[T^N](U^kW^l)}{k!l!}\\
&=[T^N]\bigl(\exp(U)\exp(W)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$
For the middle equality set $l=r-k$ and add the zero terms with $k+l>N$; for the last equality multiply the two truncated sums and use the Cauchy product formula. This also covers $N=0$, when only $k=l=0$ contributes $1$. Equality of all coefficients proves the addition identity.

source.place: §26, p. 151 (definition of the formal exponential); proof of Theorem 27.6, p. 156 (implicit addition identity); the finite truncation and binomial calculation are supplied by the second reader

proof.text: Putting $U=0$ in the defining series gives $\exp(0)=1$. Applying the addition identity to $U$ and $-U$ gives $1=\exp(0)=\exp(U)\exp(-U)$, and commutativity gives the corresponding left inverse; hence $\exp(U)$ is a unit and $\exp(-U)=\exp(U)^{-1}$.

source.place: §26, p. 151, formal exponential at zero and the inverse obtained by replacing U by -U

proof.text: For nonnegative integers $n$, the identity $\exp(nU)=\exp(U)^n$ follows by induction: at $n=0$ both sides are $1$ by step 2, and at $n+1$ step 1 gives $\exp((n+1)U)=\exp(nU)\exp(U)$. If $\varepsilon=-n$ with $n>0$, step 2 applied to $nU$ gives $\exp(\varepsilon U)=\exp(nU)^{-1}=(\exp(U)^n)^{-1}=\exp(U)^{-n}$, with integer powers taken in the group of units established in step 2. Every integer multiple of $U$ still has constant coefficient $0$ [def-weil-power-series-exponential]. Now induct on a finite index set $I$: the empty family gives $\exp(0)=1$, the empty product; adjoining $j\notin I$ gives $\exp(\sum_{i\in I}\varepsilon_iU_i+\varepsilon_jU_j)=\exp(\sum_{i\in I}\varepsilon_iU_i)\exp(\varepsilon_jU_j)$ by step 1. Substitute the induction hypothesis and the just-proved integer-power identity to obtain the required product over $I\cup\{j\}$.
